kind: Unapproved 48-item replacement draft for 4x duplicated four-test result combinations
reviewBasis: The 64 original case questions used only 16 distinct presence/absence patterns, each four times. Retain first 16 as exemplars and propose replacing 48 duplicates with varied controlled practical reasoning.
sourceReferences: AQA GCSE 8461 Practical Assessment – Food Tests
CCEA GCSE Biology Food Tests factfile

questions.originalSourcePrompt: In an independent food-sample assessment, Sample F2-01 has these results: iodine blue-black; heated Benedict's green / yellow / orange / brick-red; Biuret lilac / purple; ethanol emulsion test cloudy white emulsion. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: Iodine remains orange-brown in one fresh portion of a drink, but a separate portion gives an orange precipitate after heating with Benedict's. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Starch was detected; reducing sugar was not detected.
Reducing sugar was detected; starch was not detected.
Neither starch nor reducing sugar was detected because iodine stayed brown.
Reducing sugar was detected, and the iodine result also confirms starch.

accepted: Reducing sugar was detected; starch was not detected.

questions.scienceRationale: A positive heated Benedict's result is evidence for reducing sugar; orange-brown iodine is starch-negative.
questions.distractorRevisionNote: Replaced implausible foil with a misconception or evidence-limits foil; independently check all wrong options before approval.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: In an independent food-sample assessment, Sample F2-02 has these results: iodine orange-brown; heated Benedict's green / yellow / orange / brick-red; Biuret lilac / purple; ethanol emulsion test cloudy white emulsion. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: Biuret reagent turns lilac in a sample, while heated Benedict's solution stays blue. Which statement is supported?
options: Protein was detected, but reducing sugar was not detected.
Protein and reducing sugar were detected because both reagents were added.
Protein was not detected, but reducing sugar was detected.
The blue Benedict's result also indicates reducing sugar when Biuret is lilac.

accepted: Protein was detected, but reducing sugar was not detected.

questions.scienceRationale: The two reagents report separate nutrient groups and do not establish any lipid result.
questions.distractorRevisionNote: Replaced implausible foil with a misconception or evidence-limits foil; independently check all wrong options before approval.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: In an independent food-sample assessment, Sample F2-03 has these results: iodine blue-black; heated Benedict's remains blue; Biuret lilac / purple; ethanol emulsion test cloudy white emulsion. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: An extract is tested with iodine and Biuret: iodine becomes blue-black and Biuret turns lilac. No other tests are done. What can be concluded?
options: All four nutrient groups were detected.
Only starch was detected because lilac is a negative Biuret colour.
Starch and protein were detected, but the untested sugar and lipid must also be absent.
Starch and protein were detected; reducing sugar and lipid remain untested.

accepted: Starch and protein were detected; reducing sugar and lipid remain untested.

questions.scienceRationale: Only tested positive reactions can support conclusions; unperformed tests cannot establish absence.
questions.distractorRevisionNote: Replaced implausible foil with a misconception or evidence-limits foil; independently check all wrong options before approval.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: In an independent food-sample assessment, Sample F2-04 has these results: iodine orange-brown; heated Benedict's remains blue; Biuret lilac / purple; ethanol emulsion test cloudy white emulsion. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: A food extract gives a green Benedict's result after the prescribed water-bath heating; the water blank remains blue. How should this be recorded?
options: A green result means no reducing sugar because only brick-red is positive.
Green and blue are both negative because the tube did not become brick-red.
The food extract tested positive for reducing sugar.
The blue water blank makes a green sample result unreliable.

accepted: The food extract tested positive for reducing sugar.

questions.scienceRationale: Green is a weak positive reducing-sugar result under appropriate heating.
questions.distractorRevisionNote: Replaced implausible foil with a misconception or evidence-limits foil; independently check all wrong options before approval.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: In an independent food-sample assessment, Sample F2-05 has these results: iodine blue-black; heated Benedict's green / yellow / orange / brick-red; Biuret remains blue; ethanol emulsion test cloudy white emulsion. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: A known glucose positive-control sample remains blue with Benedict's solution after the heating stage. Which is the safest scientific interpretation?
options: The negative colour can be accepted without checking whether the positive control worked.
The procedure or reagent failed its positive control; repeat before interpreting unknown samples.
Add more Benedict's reagent to every unknown until the blue colour disappears.
Use the failed positive control to calculate the concentration of the unknowns.

accepted: The procedure or reagent failed its positive control; repeat before interpreting unknown samples.

questions.scienceRationale: A failed positive control invalidates a conclusion based on negative sample results.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: In an independent food-sample assessment, Sample F2-06 has these results: iodine orange-brown; heated Benedict's green / yellow / orange / brick-red; Biuret remains blue; ethanol emulsion test cloudy white emulsion. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: Distilled water turns lilac with Biuret reagent in the same batch used to test a food. What should happen before trusting the food result?
options: Prepare fresh reagents or clean equipment and repeat the water blank and food test.
The lilac blank can be subtracted mentally from the food colour without retesting.
The water blank establishes a positive Biuret result for every food tested.
Repeated results from the same batch rule out the possibility of contamination.

accepted: Prepare fresh reagents or clean equipment and repeat the water blank and food test.

questions.scienceRationale: A negative control ought to remain blue; a lilac blank suggests a problem.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: In an independent food-sample assessment, Sample F2-07 has these results: iodine blue-black; heated Benedict's remains blue; Biuret remains blue; ethanol emulsion test cloudy white emulsion. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: A seed's ethanol extract is already cloudy before it is added to water. What does that observation establish?
options: A cloudy ethanol extract alone is sufficient because cloudiness is always a positive emulsion endpoint.
Adding water is unnecessary if the ethanol extract does not look completely transparent.
The cloudiness shows there is no lipid because all lipids dissolve into completely clear water.
It is not yet a valid positive emulsion result; prepare a clear extract and perform the water-addition stage.

accepted: It is not yet a valid positive emulsion result; prepare a clear extract and perform the water-addition stage.

questions.scienceRationale: The emulsion endpoint is cloudiness developing on dilution of an ethanol extract with water.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: In an independent food-sample assessment, Sample F2-08 has these results: iodine orange-brown; heated Benedict's remains blue; Biuret remains blue; ethanol emulsion test cloudy white emulsion. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: A clear ethanol extract becomes cloudy white when added to water, while a correctly prepared ethanol-water blank stays clear. What is supported?
options: The emulsion was negative because the ethanol extract was initially clear.
The cloudy result identifies protein rather than lipid.
Lipid was detected in the sample.
A clear water blank confirms that the food contains reducing sugar.

accepted: Lipid was detected in the sample.

questions.scienceRationale: A clear blank with a milky sample supports a positive lipid emulsion result.
questions.distractorRevisionNote: Replaced implausible foil with a misconception or evidence-limits foil; independently check all wrong options before approval.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: In an independent food-sample assessment, Sample F2-09 has these results: iodine blue-black; heated Benedict's green / yellow / orange / brick-red; Biuret lilac / purple; ethanol emulsion test remains clear. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: A purple Biuret result is seen, but the pupil never performs an iodine test. Which statement would overreach the evidence?
options: The Biuret result supports protein being present.
The sample must contain no starch.
No iodine test result is available.
A separate iodine test is needed to assess starch.

accepted: The sample must contain no starch.

questions.scienceRationale: Protein evidence cannot prove absence of untested starch.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: In an independent food-sample assessment, Sample F2-10 has these results: iodine orange-brown; heated Benedict's green / yellow / orange / brick-red; Biuret lilac / purple; ethanol emulsion test remains clear. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: A clean water blank unexpectedly becomes blue-black when iodine is added. What is the best response?
options: Investigate contamination or a faulty control and repeat with clean water and equipment.
Accept a blue-black water blank as normal because iodine is naturally dark-coloured.
Subtract the blank's colour by eye and continue to score the original unknowns as positive.
Repeat the unknown only, without checking the blank, because food extracts cannot contaminate water.

accepted: Investigate contamination or a faulty control and repeat with clean water and equipment.

questions.scienceRationale: The water blank must not behave like a starch-positive sample.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: In an independent food-sample assessment, Sample F2-11 has these results: iodine blue-black; heated Benedict's remains blue; Biuret lilac / purple; ethanol emulsion test remains clear. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: Iodine stays orange-brown in a known starch positive-control solution. What can the pupil conclude about unknown negative-looking tubes?
options: The negative-looking unknowns are reliable because the reagent gave the same colour in every tube.
Increase the iodine added to unknown samples until a positive colour is seen.
Treat the starch control as a negative control because it stayed brown.
They cannot yet be trusted; the reagent or method needs checking.

accepted: They cannot yet be trusted; the reagent or method needs checking.

questions.scienceRationale: A failed known positive control makes negative results uncertain.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: In an independent food-sample assessment, Sample F2-12 has these results: iodine orange-brown; heated Benedict's remains blue; Biuret lilac / purple; ethanol emulsion test remains clear. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: A food remains blue in the Biuret test, while an egg-white positive control turns purple. What is the cautious conclusion?
options: A blue Biuret result proves there are absolutely no proteins, regardless of detection limits.
The food must contain protein because the positive control became purple.
Protein was not detected in the food under the test conditions.
The blue result means a Benedict's reducing-sugar test would necessarily be negative.

accepted: Protein was not detected in the food under the test conditions.

questions.scienceRationale: A valid negative supports 'not detected', not absolute absence.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: In an independent food-sample assessment, Sample F2-13 has these results: iodine blue-black; heated Benedict's green / yellow / orange / brick-red; Biuret remains blue; ethanol emulsion test remains clear. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: After suitable heating, the distilled-water Benedict's blank turns orange. Why is interpreting the food tubes risky?
options: Use the orange blank as the normal negative reference and accept all food results.
The negative control is abnormal, so contamination or a reagent problem must be investigated.
Subtract the blank colour visually from food tubes without checking contamination.
Repeat the food tubes but omit the blank because a positive blank cannot affect the inference.

accepted: The negative control is abnormal, so contamination or a reagent problem must be investigated.

questions.scienceRationale: Heated distilled water should remain blue in a working reducing-sugar test.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: In an independent food-sample assessment, Sample F2-14 has these results: iodine orange-brown; heated Benedict's green / yellow / orange / brick-red; Biuret remains blue; ethanol emulsion test remains clear. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: A pupil heats a Benedict's tube for much less time than the working glucose control and it stays blue. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The shortened heating may give a false negative; repeat with the same prescribed heating time.
Treat blue as a valid negative result even though the tube received less heat than the control.
Increase the reagent volume instead of correcting the shortened heating time.
Compare with an unheated control only and infer there is no reducing sugar.

accepted: The shortened heating may give a false negative; repeat with the same prescribed heating time.

questions.scienceRationale: Inadequate heating undermines a negative Benedict's result.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: In an independent food-sample assessment, Sample F2-15 has these results: iodine blue-black; heated Benedict's remains blue; Biuret remains blue; ethanol emulsion test remains clear. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: A properly heated Benedict's test gives yellow precipitate. A separate, correctly performed emulsion test stays clear. Which statement is supported?
options: Reducing sugar was absent because the Benedict's precipitate was yellow rather than brick-red.
Lipid was detected because the ethanol-water mixture remained clear.
A positive Benedict's colour means the lipid result must also be positive.
Reducing sugar was detected; lipid was not detected.

accepted: Reducing sugar was detected; lipid was not detected.

questions.scienceRationale: A positive yellow Benedict's result and a negative emulsion test address different substances.
questions.distractorRevisionNote: Replaced implausible foil with a misconception or evidence-limits foil; independently check all wrong options before approval.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: In an independent food-sample assessment, Sample F2-16 has these results: iodine orange-brown; heated Benedict's remains blue; Biuret remains blue; ethanol emulsion test remains clear. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: Iodine, heated Benedict's and Biuret tests are negative. The ethanol emulsion test is not performed. Which conclusion is NOT justified?
options: Starch was not detected by iodine.
Reducing sugar was not detected by heated Benedict's.
No lipids are present in the sample.
Protein was not detected by Biuret.

accepted: No lipids are present in the sample.

questions.scienceRationale: An unperformed lipid test cannot establish that lipids are absent.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: A pupil checks four substances in an unknown extract. Sample F3-01 has these results: iodine blue-black; heated Benedict's green / yellow / orange / brick-red; Biuret lilac / purple; ethanol emulsion test cloudy white emulsion. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: When comparing iodine tests on samples taken from two different bread types, which control makes the comparison fairer?
options: Use the same number of crumbs without checking their masses.
Measure the same mass of each bread sample.
Add more iodine to the bread expected to contain less starch.
Choose pieces that look equally dark even if their masses differ.

accepted: Measure the same mass of each bread sample.

questions.scienceRationale: Original draft already said 'equal portions', making the keyed 'measure the same mass' action redundant. Different sample masses can confound comparison of starch observations.

Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: Two food extracts are compared by heating each with Benedict's solution. Which reagent condition should be controlled?
options: Add the same measured volume of Benedict's solution to each equal sample volume.
Keep the total liquid volume similar by diluting only one food extract.
Add more Benedict's reagent to the food expected to contain more sugar.
Adjust reagent volume until the two tubes reach a similar colour.

accepted: Add the same measured volume of Benedict's solution to each equal sample volume.

questions.scienceRationale: Unequal reagent amounts make colour comparison less fair.
questions.distractorRevisionNote: Replaced implausible foil with a misconception or evidence-limits foil; independently check all wrong options before approval.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: A pupil checks four substances in an unknown extract. Sample F3-03 has these results: iodine blue-black; heated Benedict's remains blue; Biuret lilac / purple; ethanol emulsion test cloudy white emulsion. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: Two equal glucose extracts are heated in water baths at different temperatures. Which adjustment would best improve fair comparison?
options: Heat the lower-concentration extract longer to compensate for its lower bath temperature.
Change the volume of Benedict's solution in the cooler tube to obtain a similar colour.
Keep sample volume constant but allow the water-bath temperatures to vary.
Heat both tubes at the same controlled bath temperature.

accepted: Heat both tubes at the same controlled bath temperature.

questions.scienceRationale: Temperature is a controlled variable when comparing Benedict's reactions.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: A pupil checks four substances in an unknown extract. Sample F3-04 has these results: iodine orange-brown; heated Benedict's remains blue; Biuret lilac / purple; ethanol emulsion test cloudy white emulsion. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: One Benedict's tube is heated for 30 seconds and another for five minutes. What should the pupil change for a fair test?
options: Record the two heating durations and compare the final colours without adjustment.
Add extra Benedict's solution to the shorter-heated tube to compensate for less heating.
Use the same heating duration for both tubes.
Stop each tube as soon as it first changes colour, even if that makes heating times unequal.

accepted: Use the same heating duration for both tubes.

questions.scienceRationale: Reaction duration affects the observed Benedict's colour.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: A pupil checks four substances in an unknown extract. Sample F3-05 has these results: iodine blue-black; heated Benedict's green / yellow / orange / brick-red; Biuret remains blue; ethanol emulsion test cloudy white emulsion. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: A technician compares two fruit juices for reducing sugar. Which volume should be kept equal when loading the test tubes?
options: Keep the same volume of Benedict's solution but use different amounts of juice based on colour.
The volume of fruit-juice extract added to each tube.
Dilute the juice expected to contain more sugar before comparing it with the other.
Use more juice in whichever tube is initially paler and treat that as a fair comparison.

accepted: The volume of fruit-juice extract added to each tube.

questions.scienceRationale: Compare equal amounts of the tested material.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: A pupil checks four substances in an unknown extract. Sample F3-06 has these results: iodine orange-brown; heated Benedict's green / yellow / orange / brick-red; Biuret remains blue; ethanol emulsion test cloudy white emulsion. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: A food gives a faint starch colour in one iodine trial. Which design best tests repeatability?
options: Repeat on fresh equal-sized portions using the same iodine volume and procedure.
Look at the same tube several times and count these as independent repeat tests.
Use fresh portions but change the iodine volume until the results agree.
Repeat on different foods rather than on the food with the doubtful result.

accepted: Repeat on fresh equal-sized portions using the same iodine volume and procedure.

questions.scienceRationale: Independent repeat trials must control the method rather than copy one result.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: A pupil checks four substances in an unknown extract. Sample F3-07 has these results: iodine blue-black; heated Benedict's remains blue; Biuret remains blue; ethanol emulsion test cloudy white emulsion. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: Which material is a suitable negative control for a Biuret protein test?
options: A dilute egg-white solution prepared to make the purple colour faint.
A sugar solution made with milk, which contains some protein.
A known protein solution made from albumen.
Distilled water with the usual amount of Biuret reagent.

accepted: Distilled water with the usual amount of Biuret reagent.

questions.scienceRationale: Clean water contains no protein and should remain blue.
questions.distractorRevisionNote: Replaced implausible foil with a misconception or evidence-limits foil; independently check all wrong options before approval.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: A pupil checks four substances in an unknown extract. Sample F3-08 has these results: iodine orange-brown; heated Benedict's remains blue; Biuret remains blue; ethanol emulsion test cloudy white emulsion. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: Which material is the most useful positive control for testing whether Biuret reagent works?
options: Use an unknown food extract that stayed blue in a previous Biuret test.
Use distilled water because it should give a strong lilac reaction.
A known albumen or protein solution.
Use glucose dissolved in water because Benedict's would give a positive result.

accepted: A known albumen or protein solution.

questions.scienceRationale: A known protein sample should turn Biuret reagent lilac.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: A pupil checks four substances in an unknown extract. Sample F3-09 has these results: iodine blue-black; heated Benedict's green / yellow / orange / brick-red; Biuret lilac / purple; ethanol emulsion test remains clear. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: To confirm that iodine reagent can detect starch, which positive-control sample should be used?
options: A glucose solution that gives a positive Benedict's test.
A known starch suspension or solution.
Distilled water that is known to give a negative iodine result.
A vegetable-oil sample that gives a positive lipid test.

accepted: A known starch suspension or solution.

questions.scienceRationale: Known starch should turn iodine blue-black.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: A pupil checks four substances in an unknown extract. Sample F3-10 has these results: iodine orange-brown; heated Benedict's green / yellow / orange / brick-red; Biuret lilac / purple; ethanol emulsion test remains clear. Which of these nutrients were detected?

options: Distilled water containing no starch.
Potato extract known to turn iodine blue-black.
Glucose dissolved in a starch-containing suspension.
Bread flour that is known to contain starch.

accepted: Distilled water containing no starch.

questions.scienceRationale: Clean water should not give the positive blue-black iodine reaction.
questions.distractorRevisionNote: Replaced implausible foil with a misconception or evidence-limits foil; independently check all wrong options before approval.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: A pupil checks four substances in an unknown extract. Sample F3-11 has these results: iodine blue-black; heated Benedict's remains blue; Biuret lilac / purple; ethanol emulsion test remains clear. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: To check that the heated Benedict's test is working, what makes a good positive control?
options: Use a known starch suspension, heated with Benedict's in a water bath.
Use a known protein solution with Benedict's, omitting the heating stage.
Use a sample of distilled water as the positive control under the usual heating conditions.
A known glucose solution heated with Benedict's solution in the normal water bath.

accepted: A known glucose solution heated with Benedict's solution in the normal water bath.

questions.scienceRationale: Glucose is reducing sugar, so it should produce a positive heated Benedict's test.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: A pupil checks four substances in an unknown extract. Sample F3-12 has these results: iodine orange-brown; heated Benedict's remains blue; Biuret lilac / purple; ethanol emulsion test remains clear. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: Which negative control should normally remain blue after suitable heating with Benedict's solution?
options: A dilute glucose standard prepared to produce a weaker positive colour.
A concentrated glucose solution used as a positive control.
Distilled water mixed with Benedict's solution.
Fruit juice known to contain reducing sugar.

accepted: Distilled water mixed with Benedict's solution.

questions.scienceRationale: The water blank should be negative for reducing sugars.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: A pupil checks four substances in an unknown extract. Sample F3-13 has these results: iodine blue-black; heated Benedict's green / yellow / orange / brick-red; Biuret remains blue; ethanol emulsion test remains clear. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: Which sample can serve as a positive lipid control for the ethanol emulsion method?
options: Use a known glucose solution with the same ethanol-then-water steps.
A small known vegetable-oil sample extracted with ethanol and then added to water.
Use a known starch suspension with ethanol and water.
Use a clean water blank without any fat while retaining the emulsion method.

accepted: A small known vegetable-oil sample extracted with ethanol and then added to water.

questions.scienceRationale: Vegetable oil is lipid and should produce a milky emulsion.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: A pupil checks four substances in an unknown extract. Sample F3-14 has these results: iodine orange-brown; heated Benedict's green / yellow / orange / brick-red; Biuret remains blue; ethanol emulsion test remains clear. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: Which properly prepared negative control is most appropriate for the ethanol emulsion test?
options: Ethanol and water without food or added lipid.
Ethanol and water deliberately mixed with a few drops of vegetable oil.
A milk-fat extract added to water after shaking with ethanol.
A positive lipid control used alongside the unknown extract.

accepted: Ethanol and water without food or added lipid.

questions.scienceRationale: A blank without lipid should stay clear when ethanol and water are combined.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: A pupil checks four substances in an unknown extract. Sample F3-15 has these results: iodine blue-black; heated Benedict's remains blue; Biuret remains blue; ethanol emulsion test remains clear. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: The teacher labels four clear sample extracts A–D before adding reagents. Why is this especially important?
options: Labelling ensures the reagents cannot contaminate the other samples.
Labelling removes the need to keep a separate results table.
Labelling automatically controls the volumes of test reagent used.
Each observed reaction can be traced to the correct food sample.

accepted: Each observed reaction can be traced to the correct food sample.

questions.scienceRationale: Sample identity must be preserved through the practical.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: A pupil checks four substances in an unknown extract. Sample F3-16 has these results: iodine orange-brown; heated Benedict's remains blue; Biuret remains blue; ethanol emulsion test remains clear. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: A pipette has just transferred a glucose solution. Why use a clean pipette for a supposed sugar-free sample?
options: Rinsing a pipette briefly with the new sample is guaranteed to remove all traces of glucose.
A clear pipette must be free of glucose because dissolved sugar is colourless.
Glucose residue could make a false positive in the second sample.
Using one pipette is harmless if both extracts are later heated with the same Benedict's volume.

accepted: Glucose residue could make a false positive in the second sample.

questions.scienceRationale: Residue carries sugar and compromises the result.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: A laboratory technician checks an unknown food mixture. questions.prompt: What should a pupil do before opening ethanol for a lipid emulsion test at a bench with a lit Bunsen burner?
options: A yellow safety flame is safe to keep burning while ethanol is uncapped at the same bench.
Extinguish the burner and keep ethanol away from ignition sources.
A heatproof mat between the ethanol and flame removes the ignition risk.
Moving the ethanol bottle a few centimetres from a lit burner is sufficient.

accepted: Extinguish the burner and keep ethanol away from ignition sources.

questions.scienceRationale: Ethanol and its vapour are flammable.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: A laboratory technician checks an unknown food mixture. Sample F4-02 has these results: iodine orange-brown; heated Benedict's green / yellow / orange / brick-red; Biuret lilac / purple; ethanol emulsion test cloudy white emulsion. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: A pupil proposes heating an ethanol-food mixture to make the emulsion form faster. Which correction is best?
options: Do not heat the ethanol; shake with food, then add the clear extract to water.
Warming ethanol gently in an open tube is needed before water can produce an emulsion.
Add water first and then heat the ethanol-water mixture to obtain a stronger white emulsion.
Replace ethanol with hot water because the same lipid test result will form.

accepted: Do not heat the ethanol; shake with food, then add the clear extract to water.

questions.scienceRationale: No heating of ethanol is required; avoid fire risk.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: A laboratory technician checks an unknown food mixture. Sample F4-03 has these results: iodine blue-black; heated Benedict's remains blue; Biuret lilac / purple; ethanol emulsion test cloudy white emulsion. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: For Benedict's test, why use a hot-water bath rather than heating the bottom of a test tube over a direct flame?
options: The bath prevents the glass from getting hot enough to cause burns.
The bath guarantees every reducing-sugar sample gives the same precipitate colour.
The bath removes any need to keep heating time consistent across samples.
It gives more controlled, even heating and reduces local overheating.

accepted: It gives more controlled, even heating and reduces local overheating.

questions.scienceRationale: A water bath provides controlled indirect heating.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: A laboratory technician checks an unknown food mixture. Sample F4-04 has these results: iodine orange-brown; heated Benedict's remains blue; Biuret lilac / purple; ethanol emulsion test cloudy white emulsion. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: A pupil needs to remove a tube after heating Benedict's reagent. Which action reduces burn risk?
options: Hold the glass near its upper rim because the rim stays cool while the bottom is hot.
Use an ordinary paper tissue instead of a holder even if the tube remains very hot.
Use a test-tube holder and treat the glass as hot.
Grip the tube with fingers after lifting it straight out of the bath.

accepted: Use a test-tube holder and treat the glass as hot.

questions.scienceRationale: Heated glass and contents can cause burns.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: A laboratory technician checks an unknown food mixture. Sample F4-05 has these results: iodine blue-black; heated Benedict's green / yellow / orange / brick-red; Biuret remains blue; ethanol emulsion test cloudy white emulsion. Which of these nutrients were detected?

Away from all people, in case the hot mixture splashes.
Point the hot tube at the neighbouring pupil once the burner has been switched off.
Tilt the opening towards the holder's face because the mixture is no longer on a flame.

accepted: Away from all people, in case the hot mixture splashes.

questions.scienceRationale: Hot liquid may spit during heating or handling.

questions.prompt: What PPE protects the eyes when working with Benedict's, Biuret and ethanol reagents?
options: Suitable laboratory splash goggles.
Ordinary prescription glasses are equivalent to sealed splash goggles.
A lab coat alone prevents droplets from reaching the eyes.
Working slowly removes the need for any eye protection.

accepted: Suitable laboratory splash goggles.

questions.scienceRationale: Wear protective goggles against accidental splashes.

questions.originalSourcePrompt: A laboratory technician checks an unknown food mixture. Sample F4-07 has these results: iodine blue-black; heated Benedict's remains blue; Biuret remains blue; ethanol emulsion test cloudy white emulsion. Which of these nutrients were detected?
questions.prompt: An unknown food extract has just been tested with laboratory reagents. Why must it never be tasted?
options: If the sample looked edible before the practical, it remains safe to taste after adding reagents.
